lead.text: *Compact cards for the moments not yet covered in depth elsewhere.*

This deck extends the situation library one more layer. Each card is short — situation, best first move, and the specific thing that could still go wrong. Together with the earlier situation sections, these cover most of the professional and personal moments that will test what this book taught you.
Skim once for familiarity. Return when a real moment arrives.

entries.title: Case 1 — A Team Member Has an Accident On-Site

blocks.text: During a company off-site or work trip, a team member is injured seriously enough to need emergency care.

Call emergency services first. Then their emergency contact. Only after both, notify your leadership. Stay with the person until family or medical staff take over. Follow up personally within 24 hours regardless of your role in the organization.
Under stress, people skip the sequence. Prioritize: medical → family → work. If insurance, HR, or legal processes become part of it, engage those departments immediately with clean documentation.

entries.title: Case 2 — The Product Recall

blocks.text: Your company's product has a safety issue serious enough to require a recall. Media is asking. Customers are angry.

Announce the recall proactively — before you're forced to. Specific: which units, what to do, when the replacement or refund will happen. In plain language. Tone: acknowledgment of the failure, not defensiveness.

The temptation is to minimize scope or delay announcement. Both compound consequences. The classic Johnson & Johnson Tylenol response in 1982 is the modern textbook example of doing this well: immediate public communication, over-conservative scope, and full customer replacement.

entries.title: Case 3 — The Cyberattack in Progress

blocks.text: Your team discovers an active cyberattack on your systems — data being exfiltrated, accounts being compromised.

Isolate first (disconnect affected systems), then notify your security lead and leadership, then engage your incident response process. If you don't have one, get outside help now — do not wait until the attack is over. Preserve logs. Do not communicate externally until you have the facts.

Poorly managed cyber incidents often become worse through the response than through the original breach. Legal notification requirements vary by jurisdiction and data type; consult counsel early. Public statements before the facts are clear age badly.

entries.title: Case 4 — The Vendor Bankruptcy

blocks.text: A vendor critical to your operations announces bankruptcy. Their service will end in weeks.

Assess: what services are affected, on what timeline, what data or contracts are at risk. Then in parallel: engage alternative vendors immediately (do not wait to see if the current one survives), and negotiate with the bankruptcy administrator to preserve access to your data and any transition support.

Waiting to see 'if they get through it' loses weeks you don't have. Data-recovery in bankruptcy is often possible but requires acting fast, before the administrator prioritizes creditors over operational continuity.

entries.title: Case 5 — The Executive Departure

blocks.text: A senior executive — CEO, key VP, or founder — unexpectedly leaves the company. The team is shaken.

Get in front of the team within 24 hours. Acknowledge the reality without speculation ('here's what we know, here's what we don't'). Name the immediate impacts and who is covering what. Book weekly check-ins for the next month even if you don't feel you have news to share — presence beats content in leadership vacuums.

The temptation to under-communicate ('until we have everything figured out') is fatal. People fill silence with rumor. Better to say 'we don't know yet, and here's what we're doing about it' repeatedly than to wait for certainty.

entries.title: Case 6 — The Wildfire / Natural Disaster

blocks.text: A natural disaster is affecting the region where you or your team members live. Some are directly at risk.

Reach every person on your team within 24 hours. Confirm safety. Suspend all non-essential work immediately. Announce which deadlines are moved, which meetings are cancelled. Coordinate mutual aid within the team — those unaffected supporting those in the affected areas.

The reflexive 'keep the business running' instinct is usually wrong in the immediate aftermath. People will not be productive; performative meetings during a crisis damage trust in leadership. The 'business as usual' impulse comes from managers who are themselves not directly affected.

entries.title: Case 7 — The Sudden Windfall

blocks.text: You receive an unexpected large sum: inheritance, bonus, settlement, lottery, sale of an asset.

Do nothing with it for 30 days. Put it in a high-yield savings account. Talk to a fee-only fiduciary financial advisor before making any significant deployment. Then decide, deliberately, based on your existing goals — not on the windfall's novelty.

Windfalls trigger disproportionately bad decisions. The behavioral finance research on lottery winners is stark. The 30-day pause is what separates people who use windfalls wisely from those who don't. Do not announce publicly.

entries.title: Case 8 — The Medical Bill You Can't Understand

blocks.text: You receive a medical bill for thousands of dollars, with itemization you can't decode.

Do NOT pay it immediately. Request an itemized bill in plain-language form. Cross-check against your insurance's explanation of benefits (EOB). Contact your insurance about any discrepancy. Contact the provider's billing department about anything the insurance won't cover but seems unreasonable — hospitals frequently negotiate.

Many medical bills contain errors. Many contain line items you can dispute. Some insurance denials are procedural and reverse when appealed. The 'just pay it to make it go away' impulse costs people thousands of dollars they didn't actually owe.

entries.title: Case 9 — The Investment That's Losing Money

blocks.text: An investment you made — stock, business, real estate — is losing value. Meaningfully.

Before doing anything, ask: what has changed about the underlying case? Not the price — the case. If your original thesis is still valid, the price move is noise. If the thesis is broken, the loss is already the loss and staying in doesn't recover it. Decide based on forward-looking value, not backward-looking regret.

The sunk cost fallacy is at its most powerful during losses. So is confirmation bias — searching for reasons the thesis is still true. Get an outside perspective. Sometimes cutting your losses is the right move; sometimes patience is. The distinction is not emotional.

entries.title: Case 10 — The Family Member Who Asks for Money

blocks.text: A close family member asks for a significant loan or gift — not for the first time.

Decide before responding whether you can give the money without expecting it back, and whether you SHOULD give it based on the pattern. If yes to both: give it as a gift, not a loan (loans within families usually poison relationships). If no to either: say so kindly and specifically. Do not defer or vague-out.

The 'family loans' that most damage relationships are the ones that were never really loans — where both sides pretended one was expected back while knowing it wouldn't be. Cleaner: gift or no. Say which.

entries.title: Case 11 — The Aging Parent Who Needs More Help

blocks.text: A parent is showing signs of decline — memory, physical, or judgment — and can no longer manage alone. They resist help.

Get medical assessment first. Consult a geriatric care manager if available in your area. Involve siblings early — coordinate rather than compete. Preserve their dignity in every conversation: they are losing autonomy, not intelligence. Focus on what they can still control.

This is a marathon, not a moment. Guilt, sibling conflict, financial pressure, and grief will compound. Do not try to be the sole caregiver — professional support (in-home care, adult day programs, eventually residential) exists for good reason. Care for yourself so you can care for them.

entries.title: Case 12 — The Adult Child in Crisis

blocks.text: An adult child (yours or a close family member's) is in a real crisis — addiction, mental health, financial collapse, legal trouble.

Distinguish support from rescue. Support: consistent presence, listening, practical help with concrete needs, information about professional resources. Rescue: taking responsibility for outcomes only they can produce. The first strengthens them; the second usually prolongs the crisis.

Well-meaning parents often extend crises by removing consequences. Al-Anon, professional counseling, and books like Beyond Addiction are resources for families in this specific situation. Care for yourself too — burnout in family caregivers is its own crisis.

entries.title: Case 13 — The Sibling Who Won't Speak to You

blocks.text: A sibling has cut off contact. You don't fully understand why. Family gatherings are becoming awkward.

Reach out ONCE, directly and warmly, acknowledging the distance and asking to understand. Do not demand a response. Then wait — sometimes years. If and when they reach back, meet them where they are, not where you think they should be.

Trying to force resolution generally deepens the rift. So does bypassing them through other family members. Sustained low-pressure openness — annual birthday notes, invitations to major events without expectation — is the most reliable path back over years.

entries.title: Case 14 — The Friend Whose Politics Now Alienate You

blocks.text: A long-standing friend has moved politically or ideologically to a place you find genuinely difficult to be around. The friendship is fraying.

Distinguish disagreement from harm. Disagreement, even sharp, is compatible with friendship; harm — positions that endanger people you love or violate your core values — is not. Have one honest conversation about the specific gap. Then decide, deliberately, whether the friendship can survive by focusing elsewhere or whether it cannot.

Some friendships genuinely cannot survive certain shifts. That is a legitimate loss, and the friend's shift is not your responsibility to reverse. Others survive with re-negotiated topics of conversation. Which is which depends on the specifics — not on general rules.

entries.title: Case 15 — The Divorce

blocks.text: You are going through, or considering, divorce.

Get a good attorney — not the first one you find, and not one who promises to 'destroy' the other party. Consider mediation if the relationship allows it. Prioritize the children's welfare specifically and continuously if applicable. Do not use social media as a weapon or diary. Get therapy for yourself.

Divorces done well are still hard. Divorces done badly are catastrophic — financially, emotionally, and generationally. The instinct to 'win' at the other spouse's expense usually costs more than it gains. Focus on your own life reconstruction, not on prosecuting the past.

entries.title: Case 16 — The Bystander Moment

blocks.text: You witness something wrong — harassment, unfair treatment, a colleague being publicly demeaned. You are not the target.

Intervene safely. Simplest form: neutral interruption. 'Excuse me — can I ask a question about the previous topic?' redirects the room. Later, privately, check on the target and ask if they would like formal support. If the pattern recurs, document and escalate.

Bystander intervention is a trainable skill. Research on effective interventions — see Bystander Intervention research — consistently shows that even small redirecting moves reduce escalation. The bystander effect only holds when no one acts first.

entries.title: Case 17 — The Whistleblower Choice

blocks.text: You have direct evidence of wrongdoing in your organization — fraud, safety violations, discrimination — that internal channels have either ignored or covered up.

Consult a whistleblower-experienced attorney BEFORE acting further. In many jurisdictions there are specific protections — but only if you follow specific procedures. Document everything carefully. Do not communicate about it internally beyond channels the attorney recommends.

Whistleblowers face documented retaliation even in jurisdictions with legal protections. The personal cost is real. Whistleblower support organizations (Government Accountability Project, Whistleblower Aid, and similar in various jurisdictions) exist specifically to help navigate this. This is not a decision to make alone.

entries.title: Case 18 — The Small Lie That Would Make Everything Easier

blocks.text: A small dishonest choice — inflating a metric, obscuring a delay, taking undeserved credit — would solve the immediate problem cleanly.

Refuse. Not for the moral high ground, but for the practical reason: small lies compound. The person who lies once is now managing the lie, and the next lie that must maintain it, and the next. Take the immediate discomfort of honesty. The compounding cost of small lies is far greater than the cost of a difficult conversation now.
Sometimes 'honesty' becomes a cover for unnecessary cruelty. The distinction matters: 'radical candor' cares personally AND challenges directly. Refuse the lie without abandoning tact.

entries.title: Case 19 — The Inheritance Split

blocks.text: A parent dies. The inheritance is being divided among siblings. It's not simple.

Slow down. Almost every family inheritance conflict compounds if handled fast. Engage a professional executor or estate attorney if the estate is nontrivial. Meet with siblings together before making unilateral moves. Distinguish monetary value from sentimental value — the fights are usually about the second, dressed up as the first.
Inheritance disputes destroy more family relationships than any other cause. Ten years later, most siblings would trade the money for having handled the conversation differently. Slow is fast here.

entries.title: Case 20 — The Testimonial Someone Asks You to Falsify

blocks.text: Someone asks you to give a testimonial, reference, or endorsement that is exaggerated or false.

Decline. Cleanly. 'I'd want to give you an honest endorsement — and here's the version I could genuinely give. Would that work?' If the honest version isn't what they want, they'll go elsewhere. That is the correct outcome.
This is a repeated situation over a career. Establishing your reputation as someone whose endorsements are honest is a long-term asset. Falsifying one weakens every future endorsement you give.

entries.title: Case 21 — The AI Deepfake / Impersonation

blocks.text: You discover that someone is using AI to impersonate you — voice, image, video, or written communication.

Document everything: screenshots, links, evidence. Alert the platforms where the impersonation is occurring. Notify people who might interact with the impersonator (colleagues, family, clients). If financial fraud is possible, contact your bank. If defamatory content is being spread, consult an attorney.

AI-generated impersonation is a rapidly evolving threat and law enforcement response varies widely. Some jurisdictions have specific statutes; others are still catching up. Speed of response matters — impersonations spread faster than they can be removed.

entries.title: Case 22 — The Data Leak That Includes You

blocks.text: A company you use has a data breach. Your personal information — possibly including financial or authentication data — is compromised.

Immediately: change passwords on the affected service AND any service where you reused the password. Enable 2FA everywhere you haven't. Monitor financial accounts for unusual activity. Consider freezing credit reports if identity theft is possible. Sign up for the breach notification the company offers (usually free credit monitoring for one year).
Breaches often surface only months after they occurred. The window for damage extends. Set long-term alerts on financial accounts. Assume the compromised data is public and act accordingly.

entries.title: Case 23 — The AI Content in Your Child's Homework

blocks.text: You discover your child (or student) submitted AI-generated work as their own.

Have the conversation calmly, focused on learning rather than punishment. What was the assignment actually trying to teach? What did they lose by skipping the work? What is the specific policy at their school? Then help them submit a corrected version and, if the policy requires, self-report.

Panic-punishment produces defensive teenagers who get better at hiding rather than at doing the work. The larger conversation — when and how AI should be part of learning — is one of the central questions of modern education, and worth having thoughtfully.

entries.title: Case 24 — The Social Media Post That Blows Up Badly

blocks.text: Something you posted publicly has gone viral for the wrong reasons. Strangers are attacking you.

Do not engage. Do not defend. Do not delete immediately — screenshots already exist, and deletion often reads as guilty. Instead: post ONE clarification or apology, in your own words, if warranted. Then log off. Log OFF. For days if needed.

Responding to online pile-ons almost always escalates them. The internet's attention span is short if you stop feeding the story. If the content actually caused harm, address that harm — offline, privately, with the people actually affected. If it was misunderstood, one correction plus silence is usually the right move.

entries.title: Case 25 — The Reference Who Would Give a Great One But Is Slow

blocks.text: You need a reference for a job application by Friday. Your best reference is famously slow to respond.

Reach out at least three weeks in advance with a specific ask: 'The role is at X company. Here's the JD. Here are the three points I hope you can speak to. Deadline is Friday. Would that work?' Then follow up 48 hours before the deadline. If they still haven't responded, have a plan B ready — a good second-choice reference you've already asked contingently.

Great references are worth waiting for; unreliable references are worse than no references. Never list someone as a reference without confirming they'll respond — an unresponsive reference damages your candidacy actively.

entries.title: Case 26 — The Job Offer You Should Have Been Given

blocks.text: An internal role you thought was yours went to someone else without a fair process.

Ask for a specific debrief: what were the actual criteria, how were candidates evaluated, was there a specific gap in your candidacy? Not to argue — to understand. Then decide, with the actual information, whether to stay and address the gap or to look externally.

Some 'unfair' outcomes reveal genuine gaps you can address. Some reveal that the company's process for advancement is broken — in which case, staying is unlikely to fix it. The debrief conversation clarifies which.

entries.title: Case 27 — The Peer Who Is Being Set Up to Fail

blocks.text: You notice that a colleague is being given an impossible assignment — one where success is not realistically achievable and blame will fall on them.

Tell them privately. Not conspiratorially — colleague to colleague. 'I'm noticing X. I'm not sure it's fair. I want to make sure you see the pattern.' Then let them decide what to do. Do not intervene unilaterally on their behalf.
Sometimes what looks like a setup is actually a genuine stretch assignment that the colleague can handle. Sometimes it isn't. Either way, information is a gift; forced advocacy is not.

entries.title: Case 28 — The Manager Who Is Genuinely Wrong

blocks.text: Your manager is confidently making a decision you believe is wrong on the merits. You have specific evidence to that effect.

Push back in a targeted way. In private. With specific data. 'I want to make sure I'm not missing something — I'm seeing X, which suggests Y. What am I missing about the current plan?' If they still disagree, decide: is this the hill to escalate on, or the one to defer on and be proven right later?

Being 'right' at your manager's expense in a meeting has career consequences even when you were right. The professional move is usually to push back once in private, then either accept the call or escalate through proper channels — never to litigate in the meeting.

entries.title: Case 29 — The Person Who Wants to Be Your Mentor

blocks.text: Someone senior offers to be your mentor. You're flattered. You're not sure they're the right person.

Take one meeting. Explore what they specifically want to give you and what you specifically want from a mentor. Some 'mentors' are seeking validation more than mentoring; some are genuinely generous. The meeting will usually reveal which. Commit to a longer relationship only if the fit is real.

A mentor relationship that isn't a fit consumes time and creates awkwardness when it ends. Better to defer the commitment than to accept and later withdraw. 'I appreciate this and I want to make sure I'm being a good use of your time — let's do a couple of exploratory meetings and see how it goes' is a legitimate opening.

entries.title: Case 30 — The Startup Idea From a Friend

blocks.text: A friend pitches you their startup idea and asks for your honest opinion — or asks you to invest.

For opinions: separate the specific idea from the friend. Ask questions that would help them test it. Do not tell them it's brilliant if it isn't. Do not tell them it's terrible if you haven't done the work to know. Honest inquiry is what friends actually need. For investment: the rule is only invest what you can lose entirely without damaging either the friendship or your finances. If either would be damaged, decline kindly.

Startup ideas from friends are one of the most common ways friendships are damaged by money and one of the most common ways people lose meaningful sums. Angel investing is a professional discipline; 'investing to support a friend' is neither investing nor supporting well. Decline cleanly if either dimension isn't right.

Thirty more situations, in compact form. Combined with the earlier situation library and full cards, this book now contains detailed treatments for something like 110 real-life moments that will test the practices it teaches.

You will not memorize any specific card. What you will do — over time, if you use this book as a reference rather than a one-time read — is develop the pattern-recognition to notice when you're IN a situation this book has treated. That recognition is the beginning of the resourceful response.
The rest is practice. Which is, as it has been throughout, entirely up to you.
*“Cards do not make the resourceful person. Practice does. But the cards shorten the distance to the practice.”*
